statement: In a dietary analysis with total energy in the outcome model (standard model, or residual method with energy kept), a nutrient's coefficient estimates a substitution: more of that nutrient in place of the same energy from the energy sources not in the model, at fixed total energy, not the effect of simply eating more of it; with several energy sources in the model, 'everything else' is only the sources left out.
regime: dietary lens; nutrient exposures; a total-energy column in the outcome model; linear model
decision: how every energy-adjusted coefficient, estimand caption and energy finding is read
user_sees: An energy-adjusted coefficient is a substitution estimate: more of this nutrient and correspondingly less of everything else, at the same total intake — not the effect of simply eating more of it.
notes: Same claim at content.py:155-162 (LENS dietary), 1034-1038 (energy why), 1397-1402 (estimand drawer), 1219 (substitution why), terms 1070-1071 and 1079-1080 ('every swap is partly in its place'); finding_words.py:579-586 ('adjusting still makes each effect a swap at fixed energy'); voice.py:1334-1335 and 1490-1493 (omitted sources: 'the curve carries the confounding of the sources total energy holds as one composite'). The test covers only the omitted-sources part (a two-nutrient swap is biased; four sources recover the truth). The substitution reading assumes a linear, additive model; with splines or non-identity links it is conditional on the other intakes.

statement: With total energy also in the outcome model, replacing a nutrient by its residual on energy only reparametrizes it, so the nutrient's coefficient, interval and p-value are identical to the standard (multivariate) model's, with or without other covariates.
regime: dietary lens; linear (untransformed) residual method with energy kept; same rows for the residual and outcome models
decision: the residual method's default form (energy kept) and the 'same question' settlement of the energy model
user_sees: With total energy also in the model, swapping a nutrient for its residual only reparametrizes it, so the coefficient, its interval and p are identical to the standard model's, covariates or not
claimed_basis: McCullough & Byrd 2023; BLUEPRINT §12 ruling 1; Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS M2)
notes: Also option consequence content.py:1046-1048; BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:211-212 ('the residual method gives exactly this number') and §5 ('the standard and residual models span one space'). Missing conditions: exact only for the linear residual; within-sex (stratified) residuals put sex×energy in the column space, so the identity fails unless that term is in the outcome model (content.py:1120-1125 says the field default is within sex, on log intakes); under prediction the residual line is fit on training rows only.

statement: When total energy is dropped from the outcome model after the residual method, the nutrient's coefficient equals the standard model's only when no covariate correlates with energy, its interval is wider even then, and otherwise it differs, sometimes in sign.
regime: dietary lens; residual method, energy-dropped form; covariates in the model
decision: the 'Residual, energy dropped' option and its design warning
user_sees: With energy dropped, the coefficient is the standard model's only when no covariate correlates with energy, and its interval is wider even then; otherwise it differs, sometimes in sign.
notes: Also option 1049-1051 and voice.py:1326-1331. The test demonstrates the sign flip on one fixture only; 'equal when uncorrelated' and 'wider even then' are untested. 'Wider' needs energy to explain outcome variance; if energy is unrelated to the outcome the interval is about the same.

statement: In the log-scale residual method each nutrient is replaced by exp(its log residual on log energy plus the predicted log nutrient at mean log energy), which is the nutrient at the geometric-mean energy, so its coefficient is per unit of a rescaled nutrient at fixed energy and is not the standard model's coefficient.
regime: dietary lens; residual method with log_transform
decision: the methods sentence for the log residual
user_sees: replaced by exp(the log residual plus the predicted log nutrient at mean log energy), the nutrient at the geometric-mean energy, so a coefficient is per unit of the rescaled nutrient at fixed …
notes: The energy-dropped log variant says a coefficient 'reads like a rescaled nutrient density's' (voice.py:1326), vaguer and untested.

statement: In the all-components model (every energy source its own term in kcal), each coefficient is the total effect of adding that source's calories, a source's average substitution effect is its coefficient minus the other sources' coefficients weighted by their share of the remaining energy, and the model avoids composite-variable bias at a cost in precision.
regime: dietary lens; inference; every energy source measured in kcal
decision: the 'All components' option and the average relative effect it reports
user_sees: each coefficient is the total effect of adding that source's calories, and its average swap is the coefficient less the other sources', weighted by their share of the remaining energy (Tomova et …
claimed_basis: Tomova et al. 2022 (DISPUTED badge; Willett, Stampfer & Tobias 2022 named as disputing)
notes: Also term 1076-1078, option 1063-1064, voice.py:1347-1351. Badge here is DISPUTED, while content.py:1112-1119 (SETTLED) calls it 'the paper's recommended route'. 'Total effect' requires every source measured and no confounding. BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS §5 says all-components is refused in the sugar journey, while test_wp6::test_6b ranks it first under inference.

statement: Standard and residual energy models are biased even without confounding (composite variable bias), all four classic energy models only partly account for confounding by common dietary causes, the nutrient-density coefficient is an obscure quantity, and adding energy as a term to a density model makes it more accurate but still biased.
decision: the energy-adjustment drawer and the density options' consequences
user_sees: Standard and residual models are biased even without confounding (composite variable bias), and all four models only partly account for confounding by common dietary causes
notes: Also options 1054-1059 ('Density plus energy: obscure, and still biased'; 'Density alone: a rescaled effect whose meaning is obscure'), coach.py:400-404. 'Biased' is relative to Tomova's causal estimands; Willett et al. 2022 contest the framing, yet the badge is SETTLED beside a DISPUTED badge for all-components.

statement: Total energy drives nutrient intake through body size, activity and reporting scale, and because errors in reported nutrients and energy are correlated, they partly cancel once energy is accounted for.
decision: why the energy question is asked
user_sees: Total energy drives nutrient intake through body size, activity and reporting scale; the hypothesis is usually about composition, not quantity; and correlated reporting errors in nutrients and …
notes: Also why 1034-1036 ('the errors in reported nutrients and energy move together'). How much cancels depends on the method (density/residual vs standard) and the error correlation; with several error-prone intakes the correction's direction is not guaranteed (content.py:637-640).

statement: When the outcome is BMI, adiposity, weight, waist, body fat or diabetes, total energy is plausibly on the causal path from diet composition to the outcome and adiposity causes under-reporting of energy, so conditioning on reported energy can be over-adjustment and collider-stratification bias at once, and adjusted and unadjusted models should both be presented.
regime: dietary lens; energy-related outcome (named or read from values)
decision: the energy card's disputed note, the DISPUTED badge on the energy finding, the adjustment drawer
user_sees: Total energy is plausibly on the causal path from diet composition to adiposity, and adiposity causes under-reporting of energy. Conditioning on reported energy can then be over-adjustment and …
notes: Also content.py:1126-1131 and 1438-1444; finding_words.py:1061-1073. Tests check that the badge and text appear (test_wp15_claims.py::test_3_*), not the claim. Diabetes is in the trigger list but the causal argument is stated for adiposity.

statement: Adjusting for total energy does not by itself make a substitution isocaloric: the swapped components must be measured and analyzed in calories, and with components in grams or servings the substitution reported is not the one intended.
regime: dietary lens; substitution between two exposures
decision: whether a substitution is offered (two energy-bearing exposures required) and its unit
user_sees: Adjusting for total energy does not by itself make a substitution isocaloric. The components must be measured and analyzed in calories; in grams or servings, the substitution reported is not the …
notes: Also why 1219-1222 ('grams and servings do not make an isocaloric swap'), term 1236-1237, interview.py:313. For macronutrients in grams with energy held fixed, a coefficient is still an isocaloric swap per gram (e.g., 1 g fat = 9 kcal of the rest), so grams change the scale rather than the isocaloric property; the claim holds for gram-for-gram swaps of sources with different energy density and for servings. The Estimate beats state swaps in grams ('25 g more sugar, 25 g less other carbohydrate').

statement: On a dietary table, a nutrient whose Pearson correlation with total energy is at least 0.3 has effects 'tangled with total energy' and energy 'explains' r² of its variance (called 'most' only above r² = 0.5), while below |r| = 0.3 the nutrient 'barely tracks' energy.
regime: dietary lens; energy column settled; computed on the preview pool or, for the finding, all rows
decision: the energy-adjustment coach notes and the energy finding's summary
user_sees: `protein_g` tracks `kcal` at r `0.67`: energy explains `45%` of it
claimed_basis: audit MI-03 (r² as share of variance); TANGLED_R comment 'r ≥ 0.3 is a moderate correlation or more'
notes: Also finding_words.py:561-586 ('correlates 0.67 ... across all N rows: nutrient effects are tangled with total energy'). test_wp15_claims.py::test_8_the_coach_states_r_squared_and_says_most_only_past_half and test_wp13_recognizers.py::test_1h check the text against r*r and the threshold, not the claim. The 0.3 cut-off is unsourced; r² is the linear share only.

statement: After an energy-adjustment method is applied, an adjusted nutrient whose correlation with energy falls below |r| = 0.1 holds 'what is left is composition' (non-density methods), an unadjusted nutrient 'still carries how much people eat', and an unchanged correlation under the standard model is because energy enters the model beside it.
decision: the energy-adjustment preview's coach notes
user_sees: With this method r `0.00`: what is left is composition.
notes: test_coach.py checks the text only. A residual has r = 0 with energy on the rows it was fit on by construction, so the note is near-tautological; 'composition' is an interpretation beyond what r measures (ledger #81 already withdrew it for densities).

statement: When a unit's rows are repeated measurements of one quantity, averaging k of them cuts within-person variance k-fold.
regime: repeated rows answered 'repeats' (e.g., 24-hour recalls); aggregation by mean; k = the median rows per unit
decision: the aggregation preview's coach note
user_sees: Averaging `2` replicates cuts within-person variance `2`-fold.
notes: test_coach.py:143 checks the text only. True only for the error variance of a person's mean, and only if replicate errors are independent with equal variance; content.py:557-561 says consecutive-day recalls have correlated errors, so the cut is smaller. 'Within-person variance' itself does not change; k is the median count, not each unit's.

statement: Averaging replicates of one quantity (e.g., two 24-hour recalls days apart) reduces day-to-day error, while averaging time points (e.g., clinic visits months apart) erases the change between them, which is the signal.
regime: repeated rows per unit; aggregation question
decision: the aggregation menu's order (mean first for repeats, not for time points)
user_sees: Replicates of one quantity can be averaged; time points carry change that averaging would erase.
notes: Also one-liner 603-604, options 535-539 and 614-615, coach.py:496-497 ('Averaging `k` time points erases change between them'). Whether order is 'the signal' depends on the estimand: for a between-person association with a stable trait, averaging visits can be appropriate.

statement: 24-hour recalls on consecutive days have correlated errors, so within-person variation is underestimated and the data look more reliable than they are.
decision: the repeats question's drawer
user_sees: Recalls on consecutive days have correlated errors, so within-person variation is underestimated and the data look more reliable than they are. NHANES uses non-consecutive days by design.
notes: This contradicts the independence the coach note (D-012) assumes.

statement: The mean of a person's available recalls, as the model's only error-prone exposure under classical error, gives a coefficient attenuated toward zero, but with several error-prone nutrients or energy in the model a coefficient can be attenuated, inflated or change sign.
regime: dietary lens; repeated recalls averaged; regression on the mean
decision: the aggregation card's why and drawer
user_sees: Under classical error it is attenuated toward zero only as the model's one error-prone study factor: with several error-prone nutrients, or energy, in the model, a coefficient can be attenuated …
claimed_basis: Keogh et al. 2020 (STRATOS); Freedman et al. 2011 (CONVENTION badge)
notes: Also why 606-610, term 623-624 ('averaging more days reduces it'), BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:671-673. The test shows the sign flip with two exposures; the single-exposure attenuation is not tested.

statement: With repeated rows per person, a row-level split puts one person's rows on both sides, so the model is scored on people it has already seen and every score is inflated; splits must keep each participant's rows together.
regime: repeated rows per participant (recalls, visits, samples)
decision: the grain question, the seal's grouping and every fold
user_sees: With repeated recalls, a row-level split puts one person's days on both sides and inflates every score. Split by participant, not by row.
notes: Also content.py:489-492, 590-594, 684-687, 1005-1008, 1363-1367; finding_words.py:1168-1175 ('lets a model recognize people instead of learning, and every score looks better than it is'). Behavioral tests exist (no unit spans folds), none shows the inflation. 'Every score is inflated' is overstated when person-level information is weak; the size depends on within-person correlation and model capacity.

statement: Under prediction, internal validation must resample the entire modeling pipeline, so every step learned from data (energy-adjustment residuals, scaling, imputation, PCA loadings, feature ranking and selection, thresholds, tuning) is fit inside each training fold; selecting features on all samples can report near-zero error when no signal exists.
regime: prediction; any table; cross-validation or bootstrap
decision: the fit pipeline (every learned step in-fold) and the split drawers
user_sees: Internal validation must resample the entire modeling pipeline: imputation, transformation, selection and tuning.
claimed_basis: CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK §A5.5 (SETTLED); GENOMICS_PACK §08 (Ambroise & McLachlan 2002); WHAT_EXPLORATION_MAY_DECIDE §5.3 (Hornung 2015; Moscovich & Rosset 2022)
notes: Also content.py:471-475, 1009-1013 (near-zero error), 1132-1136 ('fitting it on all rows before cross-validation leaks the held-out rows into every fold'), 1363-1367. Under inference the app fits outcome-free steps on all rows (WHAT_EXPLORATION row 1), consistent with this being a prediction rule.

statement: For internal validation at typical clinical sample sizes, bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default, repeated cross-validation is acceptable, and a single train/test split is the weakest option.
decision: the validation scheme's order on the seal card
user_sees: Bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default and repeated cross-validation is acceptable; a single train and test split is the weakest option at typical clinical sample sizes.
notes: 'Typical clinical sample sizes' undefined. The app itself does not apply the bootstrap to boosted trees or forests (D-022), and BEATS_PREDICT §17.2 recommends a single sealed latest period under Predict; the seal card offers 10–30% holdouts.

statement: When the task predicts a later outcome from earlier measurements, a random split is optimistic, and holding out those seen last is a distinct check (validation in time) that reporting guidelines treat separately from validation on random rows.
regime: prediction; repeated rows with a time column, or a forward-looking task
decision: the temporal question: chronological seal and time-ordered folds
user_sees: A random split is optimistic when the task looks forward; the held-out people should then be those seen last.
notes: 'Optimistic' assumes drift over time. Whole units are held out by their last observation, so their earlier rows can predate training rows (term 680-681; voice.py:1227-1249).

statement: A small held-out set measures performance imprecisely, so with few rows cross-validation alone should come first, and a larger holdout gives a steadier final score at the cost of fewer training rows.
decision: the seal options' order and consequences
user_sees: A small holdout measures little, so with few rows cross-validation alone comes first.
notes: Option 978-979: 'Hold out 30%: a steadier final score, fewer rows to train.' 'Few rows' is undefined.

statement: Each cross-validated score's standard error, and the interval for each pair of families' difference (the corrected repeated k-fold t over at least 10 × K folds), computed on the user's rows, tell whether two models differ, in place of a rule about sample size.
decision: family comparison verdicts
user_sees: Each cross-validated score carries its standard error, and each pair of families an interval for their difference, computed on these rows. Read whether two models differ from that interval
notes: test_ms6_prediction_validation.py::test_2_the_corrected_repeated_kfold_t_matches_a_numpy_hand_computation checks the arithmetic only. No unbiased estimator of CV variance exists (Bengio & Grandvalet 2004); the corrected t is a heuristic with approximate coverage. BEATS_PREDICT ruling 4 says 'not distinguishable' is never read from an interval crossing zero alone, in tension with 'read whether two models differ from that interval'.

statement: Harrell's bootstrap optimism correction, with the whole pipeline refit on each resample, is sound for regression-type families, but for a family that nearly memorizes its rows (boosted trees) it understates the optimism and overstates performance, so that family's cross-validated score stands instead.
decision: which families get an optimism-corrected score
user_sees: except for a family that nearly memorizes its rows (boosted trees), whose cross-validated score stands because the bootstrap overstates it
claimed_basis: Coley et al. 2023, BMC Med Res Methodol 23:33; models/validation.py:24-32
notes: Term content.py:995-997. Forests also declare the exception (models/forest.py:328) but the sentence names only boosted trees. 'Sound for regression-type families' is tested only for logistic regression.

statement: With no rows held out and several families compared, bootstrap bias-corrected cross-validation corrects the optimism of choosing the best family, and that selection-corrected estimate, not the best family's own score, is the reported result.
regime: prediction; two or more families; no holdout (or before the seal opens)
decision: the reported performance result
user_sees: with no rows held out, the choice among them is corrected by bootstrap bias-corrected cross-validation (Tsamardinos et al. 2018), and that selection-corrected estimate is the reported result
notes: BEATS_PREDICT.md:911 and §6 item 8 turn a small correction into 'Choosing the best of three flatters it by nothing measurable here', a reading of a noisy estimate. WHAT_EXPLORATION §5.14: nested CV estimates the procedure's performance, not the chosen family's.

statement: A cross-validated or held-out R² for a regression outcome is measured against the training rows' mean and pooled over every out-of-fold prediction.
decision: the R² the Results report
user_sees: R² was measured against the training rows' mean and pooled over every out-of-fold prediction
notes: Conflicts with BEATS_PREDICT §17 ruling 7 (D-025), which computes the opened cycle's R² against the cycle's own mean; test_modeling.py:213 asserts the training-mean convention.

statement: Under Predict with a period held out, R² on the opened period computed against that period's own mean is conventional and conservative, and the comparison with a deployable baseline is the RMSE against the development mean's RMSE.
regime: prediction; a sealed latest period (NHANES glucose capture)
decision: the opened cycle's R² in Results
user_sees: R² on the opened cycle is computed against the cycle's own mean (0.18): conventional and conservative.
notes: Contradicts the engine (voice.py:1210; test_modeling.py:213 'not the held-out rows' own') and BEATS_PREDICT R5 Table 2 ('R² 0.20 ... against the development mean'). An own-mean R² ignores calibration-in-the-large; 'conservative' holds only when the period's mean differs from the development mean.

statement: Binary models should be judged on calibration as well as discrimination, because a well-calibrated model with a lower AUC can be more useful than a miscalibrated one with a higher AUC; ranking families by log loss, a strictly proper score, rewards calibrated probabilities.
decision: the ranking metric (log loss) with AUC as headline
user_sees: a well-calibrated model with a lower AUC can be more useful than a miscalibrated one with a higher AUC (Van Calster et al. 2019). ... ranks the families on log loss, a strictly proper score that …
claimed_basis: Van Calster et al. 2019, BMC Med 17:230; CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK §A5.1 (SETTLED)
notes: Also task options 359-365 and term 1184-1185 ('two models with the same AUC can differ greatly in it'). The test covers the same-ranking case; log loss trades discrimination against calibration, so it need not pick the better-calibrated of two models that rank differently.

statement: For a rare binary event, undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE overestimate the minority class's probability without improving discrimination; a rare event's real problem is small-sample overfitting, answered by penalization and sample size.
regime: binary outcome with a rare event
decision: the event card's drawer (no resampling offered)
user_sees: Undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE overestimate the probability of the minority class without improving discrimination.
notes: Shown for logistic regression (van den Goorbergh et al. 2022); for some tree learners the discrimination result varies.

statement: With more features than samples, an unpenalized least-squares or logistic model is degenerate, with infinitely many coefficient vectors fitting the data exactly, so penalization, dimension reduction or one test per feature are the ways through, the elastic net being the standard choice if one model must be named.
decision: the genomics finding's route to penalized models and the model-family drawer
user_sees: With more features than samples, an unpenalized least-squares or logistic model is degenerate rather than merely overfit: infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the data exactly.
notes: Also finding_words.py:607-612 ('count columns against samples: an unpenalized model has no unique fit'). For logistic regression the MLE typically does not exist (separation) rather than 'infinitely many fit exactly'; the test covers least squares only. With an intercept the degeneracy begins at p ≥ n.

statement: In MAQC-II (over 30,000 models from 36 teams), performance depended mainly on the endpoint and the team's proficiency and different algorithms performed similarly, so the algorithm matters less than the endpoint and the analyst.
decision: the model-families card's why
user_sees: In one comparison of 30,000 models, the algorithm mattered less than the endpoint and the analyst.
claimed_basis: GENOMICS_PACK §08 (DISPUTED in the drawer at 1193-1198); MAQC-II (Shi et al. 2010)
notes: The why line states it unhedged on every lens's family card while the drawer badges it DISPUTED; MAQC-II was microarray classification, so generalizing it to tabular diet or clinical data is outside its regime.

statement: An elastic net shrinks correlated nutrients together, which suits diets where nutrients travel in foods, while automatic selection among correlated nutrients picks one marker of a shared source rather than a cause, so selection frequency across resamples should be reported rather than a single set.
decision: the model-families card
user_sees: An elastic net shrinks correlated nutrients together, which suits diets where nutrients travel in foods.
notes: The grouping effect comes from the L2 part (Zou & Hastie 2005); with a large L1 share the elastic net still selects among highly correlated predictors.

statement: For an ordered outcome such as a 1–5 rating, a cumulative-link (proportional-odds) model uses the full ordering and handles ties, whereas a linear model on the score assumes equal gaps, and a responder split or unordered classification discards the order.
decision: the task question (ordinal task, proportional-odds model)
user_sees: An ordered score, such as a 1–5 rating, is ordinal: regression would assume equal gaps, and classification would discard the order.
notes: Also option 366-367 and term 377-378 ('best modeled by a cumulative link model', unconditional). Proportional odds is itself an assumption the claim does not mention.

statement: In a randomized trial, covariate adjustment only sharpens precision and causal wording is allowed; a case-control sample cannot give prevalence or absolute risk; matched sets are analyzed within each set; an observational study adjusts for confounders and speaks of associations.
decision: the design question, which gates adjustment and claim wording
user_sees: In a randomized trial adjustment only sharpens precision and causal wording is allowed; a case-control sample cannot give prevalence or absolute risk; matched sets are analyzed within each set.
claimed_basis: none stated (the drawer cites STROBE-nut only for naming the design)
notes: For non-collapsible measures (odds and hazard ratios) adjustment in a trial changes the estimand and can widen the interval, which the app's own term says (content.py:1393-1394, D-059); 'only' is overstated. Case-control data can give absolute risk when sampling fractions are known. Trial designs are 'Not available yet', so this is explanatory for now.

statement: A missing-value indicator is legitimate for prediction, often improving performance because the same indicator is observable when the model is used, but gives biased estimates for inference in observational data, while in a randomized trial it is valid for baseline covariates.
regime: missing predictor values; purpose prediction vs inference
decision: the missing-values question (indicators blocked under inference until recorded)
user_sees: For prediction, a missing-value indicator is legitimate and often improves performance, because the same indicator is observable when the model is used. For inference in observational data it gives …
notes: Also why 439-443 and methods/missing.py INDICATOR_CAUTION via voice.py:1070-1075 ('almost always biases'); Groenwold says 'typically'. For prediction, indicators help only if missingness at use mirrors development (Sperrin et al. 2020). BEATS_PREDICT §17.4 fills upstream-imputed values without indicators.

statement: Under inference, missing predictors should be multiply imputed with the outcome (and total energy) in the imputation model and pooled by Rubin's rules, whereas under prediction they should be imputed inside each training fold without the outcome so the fitted pipeline can impute a new row as it was developed.
decision: the missing-values question's default by purpose
location: turbotab/core/methods/missing.py:69-74 (RULE, shown in the drawer at teaching/content.py:934)
user_sees: Under inference, missing predictors are multiply imputed with the outcome and total energy in the imputation model, and the analyses pooled by Rubin's rules (Moons et al. 2006, via Harrell). Under …
claimed_basis: Moons et al. 2006; Sisk et al. 2023 (SETTLED)
notes: Also content.py:904-910, 913-920, term 930-931 (MAR). The test covers the inference half under MAR only.

statement: Multiple imputation uses m = 20 imputations, or the percentage of rows with an imputed value if that is larger.
decision: the number of imputations
user_sees: m = 20 or the percentage of rows with an imputed value if that is larger
notes: The missing-values card's option says 'each blank imputed 20 times' (content.py:914-915), which contradicts the rule when more than 20% of rows have a blank. White et al.'s rule of thumb is m at least the percentage of incomplete cases.

statement: Complete-case analysis gives unbiased regression coefficients only if whether a value is missing does not depend on the outcome, given the predictors.
decision: the methods sentence's stated assumption
user_sees: complete cases give unbiased coefficients only if whether a value is missing does not depend on the outcome, given the predictors (Groenwold et al. 2012; White & Carlin 2010)
notes: The stated condition is sufficient, not necessary: for logistic regression, missingness that depends only on the outcome leaves odds ratios (not the intercept) unbiased. test_wp7_missing_data.py::test_1 checks only the 'if' direction on one design. Term content.py:923-924 ('can bias estimates when who is missing depends on the outcome') is the softer version.

statement: On a food-frequency questionnaire a blank frequently means 'never', especially among older participants, so that missingness is not at random, and standard multiple imputation, which assumes it is, is an improvement but not a solution.
decision: the missing-values drawer
user_sees: On a food-frequency questionnaire a blank frequently means never, especially among older participants. That missingness is not at random, and standard multiple imputation assumes it is: an …
notes: 'An improvement' over what is unstated (complete cases?). Quest noticing diet-ffq-blank-means-never.

statement: For inference, filling missing predictors with the mean or median understates variance and biases coefficients whenever who is missing depends on another variable, so it is blocked until recorded, while for prediction a fill learned in each training fold is the deployable choice.
decision: median fill blocked under inference unless recorded
user_sees: For inference, mean or median filling understates variance and biases coefficients; the clinical pack calls it indefensible in a manuscript, and here it is blocked until recorded.
notes: The test measures median-fill bias (+59%, coverage 0) when blanks depend on the exposure. Term content.py:928-929. With MCAR blanks in a single X, a mean fill leaves the simple-regression slope unbiased, so 'biases coefficients' is conditional.

statement: A value missing because it is below a detection limit is small, not unknown, so a median fill wrongly puts it mid-distribution; half the minimum is customary but collapses every non-detect to one point and deflates variance, and a censoring-aware fill is sound for associations.
regime: metabolomics/lab values below a detection limit
decision: non-detection handling (median fill refused unless given a reason)
user_sees: A blank below a detection limit is small, not unknown: the median puts it in the middle of the distribution. Half the minimum is customary; a censoring-aware fill is sound for associations.
claimed_basis: METABOLOMICS_PACK §03 (SETTLED here; CONVENTION in the lens drawer 169-173)
notes: Three different 'half' rules are stated: half the feature's minimum (content.py:170, 952), 'half the limit, or the limit over √2' (finding_words.py:307-309), 'half the column's smallest detected value' (voice.py:1115-1117). The test shows half-minimum far off (0.14 against 0.5) in its scenario.

statement: In metabolomics data, missing values that cluster in the lowest-abundance features are likely below detection and not missing at random.
decision: the left-censoring finding's route to the non-detection fill
user_sees: Missing values cluster in the lowest-abundance features: likely below detection, not missing at random.
notes: Low-abundance missingness can also come from peak-picking or alignment failures (MAR/MCAR); the detector's threshold lives in the pack.

statement: A clinical reference interval holds the central 95% of healthy people by construction and is for annotation only, plausibility bounds flag values no living patient could have, and no generic outlier rule tells the two apart.
decision: the lens and repairs drawers
user_sees: A reference interval holds the central 95% of healthy people by construction and is for annotation only. Plausibility bounds flag values no living patient could have.
notes: Also content.py:254-258.

statement: In a clinical lab column, values outside the plausibility band are impossible, while values outside the reference sample's central range but inside the band are 'unusual but real'.
decision: the finding's summary and its route to exclusions
user_sees: `col` has `N` impossible values outside `lo`–`hi`; `M` more are unusual but real.
claimed_basis: audit IN-09 (code comment: 'outside the reference sample's central 98%')
notes: 'Real' asserts the values are genuine, which a range check cannot establish (entry and unit errors fall inside the band). The comment's 98% differs from the teaching's 95% reference interval (content.py:164).

statement: On a 1–5 item a code such as 9 is 'don't know' or 'refused', not an extreme answer, and sentinel codes must be recoded but never automatically, since some legitimate scales run 0–9.
regime: survey and clinical items with numeric codes
decision: the sentinel repair (offered, never applied automatically)
user_sees: In a 1–5 item, a 9 is not extremely agree; it is don't know or refused. Sentinels must be recoded, never automatically: some legitimate scales do run 0–9.
notes: Also why 229-231; finding_words.py:836-847.

statement: A TNTC ('too numerous to count') plate count is right-censored above the countable range (15–300 colonies per plate in FDA's BAM, 2026 edition), not missing, whereas QNS or a hemolyzed specimen is a measurement failure with no value and is treated as missing.
regime: clinical lens; microbiology and lab results
decision: TNTC kept as censored rather than routed to missing
user_sees: TNTC, too numerous to count, means a plate held more colonies than its countable range, 15–300 per plate in FDA's Bacteriological Analytical Manual (2026 edition)
notes: Also finding_words.py:224-306. test_wp15_claims.py::test_4_tntc_* check the text. A hemolyzed specimen can still give values for some analytes.

statement: A column unique on every row names a row or participant, and as a predictor it cannot generalize: noise at best and a way to memorize rows at worst.
regime: any table with a unique identifier column
decision: the identifier finding and role (never a predictor)
user_sees: A value that appears once cannot tell a model anything about a row it has not seen.
notes: Also content.py:699 and 733-734. A sequential identifier can carry time, order or site information, so it can generalize spuriously; the claim is about the value, not its order.

statement: A flag column (e.g., imputed_weight) describes how a value was filled rather than measuring the participant, so as a predictor it lets a model learn the filling process rather than what values measure, and it stays out of the predictors.
decision: the flag finding and role (kept out of the predictors)
user_sees: As a predictor, a flag lets a model learn how values were filled rather than what they measure.
notes: Also content.py:699-703; BEATS_PREDICT §17.4 applies the same reasoning (D-073). Under prediction, informative-missingness flags can legitimately help (content.py:464-467 says indicators are legitimate for prediction), a tension.

statement: Because NHANES oversamples some age, race and income groups, unweighted estimates describe the sample rather than the population, are biased toward the oversampled groups and can even change sign, and intervals that ignore strata and PSUs are too narrow because rows in a PSU resemble each other.
decision: the survey question and the 'no survey design' finding
user_sees: A survey oversamples some groups on purpose, so an unweighted estimate describes the sample, not the population, and can even change sign.
claimed_basis: NUTRITION_PACK §01 (SETTLED); NCHS (variance under SRS 'generally too low')
notes: Also content.py:737-744, 790-795; finding_words.py:762-764 and 1233-1240 ('results describe these participants, not the US population'). For regression coefficients (as opposed to means), unweighted estimates are not necessarily biased when the model is correct and sampling is ignorable given the covariates.

statement: NHANES dietary analyses use WTDRD1 for day 1 or WTDR2D for both days, not the exam weight WTMEC2YR, and in general the analysis takes the weight of the smallest subsample that includes every variable analyzed (e.g., a fasting or OGTT subsample weight).
regime: NHANES tables with survey weights; inference
decision: which weight the survey-weights finding recommends
user_sees: Fasting analytes set the weight: `WTSAF2YR`, not `WTDRD1`; as design columns none becomes a predictor.
claimed_basis: NHANES weighting tutorial ('least common denominator'); NHANES OGTT_I documentation (CONVENTION badge)
notes: Also content.py:740-741. When a subsample's analytes cannot be told from names, the finding says the rule may name another weight.

statement: When pooling NHANES cycles from 2001–2002 on, the two-year weights are divided by the number of cycles combined, and the 1999–2002 rows instead take the four-year weight, doubled, before that division, because the 1999–2000 and 2001–2002 weights rest on different censuses.
decision: the analysis weights under the population answer
user_sees: Combining NHANES cycles from 2001–2002 on means dividing the two-year weights by the number of cycles combined. 1999–2000 is the exception
notes: Also finding_words.py:1262-1266 and voice.py:2352-2358.

statement: Under a population survey design, a subgroup analysis keeps every row and marks the domain, since deleting rows drops PSUs and strata from the variance and gives wrong standard errors; variances are Taylor-linearized with first-stage units sampled with replacement and t intervals on the PSUs minus the strata holding the domain's rows.
regime: survey design with weights, strata and PSUs; exclusions or complete cases under the population answer
decision: domain analysis for every restriction
user_sees: To restrict to a subgroup, keep every row and mark the subgroup ... Deleting rows drops PSUs and strata from the variance and gives wrong standard errors.
notes: Also voice.py:897-904 and 2408-2413; term content.py:785-786. Deleting rows does not always change the SEs materially; the df rule is NCHS's convention.

statement: A stratum with one PSU has no between-PSU spread for Taylor linearization, and centering its PSU total at the mean PSU total (R survey lonely.psu 'adjust', Stata singleunit(centered)) is conservative.
regime: survey design with a single-PSU stratum
decision: the lonely-PSU rule in the design-based variance
user_sees: TurboTab centers such a stratum at the mean of all PSU totals (R's lonely.psu "adjust", Stata's singleunit(centered)), which is conservative, and names the stratum.
notes: voice.py:2391-2395 says 'the mean PSU total of the strata holding analysis rows', a different centering denominator from 'all PSU totals'. finding_words.py:774-777 says a lonely PSU 'breaks design-based variance estimates'. The test shows SEs at least R's 'remove' on one fixture, not conservativeness against the true variance.

statement: Under-reporting of energy is systematic and concentrated among people with higher BMI and weight-conscious participants, so excluding under-reporters when the outcome is adiposity removes a non-random slice of the studied population, which is why many analyses keep everyone.
regime: dietary lens; intake screens; adiposity-related outcomes
decision: the exclusions card's why, term and drawer
user_sees: Under-reporting is concentrated in people with higher BMI, so excluding under-reporters when the outcome is adiposity removes a non-random slice of exactly the population studied.
notes: Also content.py:819-822 and term 850-851; coach.py:271-282 compares the excluded and kept rows' median BMI.

statement: An eligibility cut chosen by looking at the outcome is data-driven selection with its own bias, so the eligibility question withholds the outcome's distribution and a custom range never applies to the outcome.
decision: outcome distribution withheld at eligibility
user_sees: A restriction comes from your research question, so the outcome's distribution is not shown here.
notes: Option content.py:842-843 ('never the outcome').

statement: Willett's textbook (2013) gives plausible-intake bounds of 500–3,500 kcal/day for women and 800–4,000 for men, the Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-up Study use 500–3,500 and 800–4,200, and variants use sex-neutral 500–5,000 or 500–3,500.
decision: the exclusion presets offered
user_sees: Willett's textbook (2013) gives 500–3,500 kcal a day for women and 800–4,000 for men.
claimed_basis: Banna et al. 2017 quoting Willett 2013; Pan et al. 2011 AJCN 94:1088 (CONVENTION)
notes: Options 830-841. test_wp15_claims.py::test_8_the_sex_specific_presets... checks counting with the stated bounds, not the attribution. The bounds were set for usual intake from FFQs; applied to single 24-hour recall days they screen days, not persons (see D-055).

statement: A row whose total energy is below 500 or above 5,000 kcal a day (2,092–20,920 kJ) is 'likely under-reporting' or 'likely over-reporting', once the column's energy role, unit and days are settled.
regime: dietary lens; one day's energy intake; settled unit
decision: the exclusions card's coach line and the implausible-intake finding
user_sees: `194` rows below `500` kcal: likely under-reporting.
claimed_basis: packs.py:2897 _PLAUSIBLE_KCAL = (500, 5000), 'the detector's own range'; no citation
notes: Also coach.py:215-236 and finding_words.py:508-519 ('N records report an implausible daily intake'). A single recall day under 500 kcal can be a true low day (illness, fasting); BEATS_PREDICT beat D keeps 'the 501 days outside 500 to 5,000 kcal ... the model will meet such days in use'; noticing diet-implausible-day-vs-person. The range is sex-neutral and adult-only, so children's intakes would be flagged.

statement: When an intake screen would remove more than half the rows, the column's unit (kJ, a multi-day total, a child's or athlete's intake) is the likelier error rather than the people, so the screens refuse to remove more than half the rows until the unit is stated.
decision: the screens' refusal and the unit question
user_sees: When a screen would remove more than half the rows, the unit is the likelier error, not the people
notes: Also coach.py:659-664 ('check the unit'). The 50% threshold is a heuristic.

statement: When follow-up ends before the event for some people, a yes/no model counts them as event-free and can manufacture an association, while a time-to-event model keeps each person for the time they were followed.
regime: binary outcome with a follow-up time that varies
decision: the follow-up question's route to a time-to-event (Cox) analysis
user_sees: A yes/no model treats them as event-free and can manufacture an association; a time-to-event model keeps each person for the time they were followed (PROBAST, item 4.6).
notes: One-liner 1309-1310. 'Manufacture' requires follow-up length to be associated with the predictors.

statement: Under inference, a site that differs in both the exposure and the outcome confounds the estimate and intervals that treat its participants as independent are too narrow, so each site gets its own intercept and cluster-robust intervals (few groups needing a small-sample correction), 'cluster only' leaves between-group differences in the estimate, and under prediction validation keeps a group together.
regime: participants grouped in sites, households or batches
decision: the grouping question's options
user_sees: Under inference a site that differs in both what you study and the outcome confounds the estimate, and intervals that treat its participants as independent are too narrow
claimed_basis: none stated (the drawer cites NUTRITION_PACK §08 for split hygiene)
notes: Options 1348-1354; term 1359-1360; finding_words.py:1155-1160; voice.py:1825-1829. Site fixed effects remove only site-level confounding.

statement: An odds ratio or hazard ratio changes when a covariate that predicts the outcome is added, even without confounding, so such an estimate is stated 'given the adjustment set', and a marginal measure comes from g-computation with the conditional odds ratio beside it.
decision: the estimand caption and the measure reported
user_sees: An odds or hazard ratio changes when a covariate that predicts the outcome is added, even without confounding.
notes: voice.py:1917-1922. Conflicts with D-032 ('in a randomized trial adjustment only sharpens precision').

statement: A direct effect holds the mediators fixed and needs the confounders of the mediator–outcome relationship adjusted too, and if an exposure–mediator interaction is not ruled out the direct effect holds only at the mediators' reference level.
decision: the adjustment set under a direct effect
user_sees: a direct effect holds the mediators fixed and needs their confounders adjusted too
notes: Also content.py:1384-1389 and voice.py:1985-1990 ('the direct effect is at its reference level only'). If a mediator–outcome confounder is itself affected by the exposure, regression cannot identify the controlled direct effect (g-methods needed); this is unstated.

statement: Statistics cannot tell a mediator from a confounder, only causal knowledge can, so covariates are chosen by the disjunctive cause criterion: adjust for causes of the exposure or the outcome, leave out instruments and consequences of the exposure, and estimate a covariate of unknown timing with and without it; adjusting for a collider can create a non-causal association and adjusting for an instrument amplifies remaining confounding.
decision: each covariate's derived role in the adjustment set
user_sees: Statistics cannot tell a mediator from something else that could explain the link; only what causes what can (VanderWeele 2019). So the disjunctive cause criterion is asked
notes: Terms 1428-1435; voice.py:1934-2000. VanderWeele's criterion also includes proxies of common causes and is sufficient when some subset of measured covariates suffices; neither condition is stated.

statement: Double machine learning and targeted maximum likelihood estimate the declared effect without assuming the outcome model's form, with cross-fitting keeping the intervals valid, but they still rest on no unmeasured confounding, positivity, consistency and time ordering; a doubly robust estimator is consistent when either the outcome or the propensity model is right, and post-double-selection lasso intervals stay valid.
regime: inference; numeric or yes/no exposure; causal lane
decision: the causal question and its top-ranked estimator
user_sees: Double machine learning and targeted maximum likelihood learn the outcome and what you study flexibly, cross-fitted so the intervals stay valid.
notes: Options 1466-1473, terms 1478-1483. Valid DML/TMLE intervals also need the nuisance estimators to converge fast enough (product rate faster than n^-1/2) and adequate overlap; PDS-lasso needs approximate sparsity. Neither is stated.

statement: When a time-varying confounder was itself affected by earlier exposure, standard regression is biased whether it adjusts for that confounder or not, while marginal structural models with inverse-probability weights or the parametric g-formula adjust for it at each time point; stabilized weights should average near 1.
regime: inference; exposure varying within units over time points
decision: the time-varying question's options
user_sees: standard regression is biased either way: adjusting for it removes part of the effect, and leaving it out leaves the later values confounded (Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000).
notes: Terms 1531-1536. A mean near 1 is necessary, not sufficient (Cole & Hernán).

statement: For a continuous exposure or confounder, a straight line the truth does not follow biases the estimate and a confounder cut into a few groups leaves residual confounding, and choosing the form after seeing a nonlinearity test inflates the test of association (by about 50% in Grambsch & O'Brien), so the form is declared before estimates and its overall test is reported.
decision: the form question (spline by default, declared before estimates)
user_sees: Choosing the form after seeing a nonlinearity test inflates the test of association, so the form is declared first and its overall test is the one reported.
notes: BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:648 ('it bends' when p < 0.05) and M4 ('if the truth bends, it averages over the bend'); in the Estimate journey the straight line stays the estimate after the planned check rejects linearity.

statement: Restricted cubic splines use 3–5 knots at Harrell's percentiles (3 at 10/50/90, 4 at 5/35/65/95) of the values the model sees, with k chosen by Harrell's rule on the effective sample size (k = 3 for n < 30, k = 5 for n ≥ 100) and quintiles reported alongside.
decision: knot count and placement
user_sees: Restricted cubic spline of outcome vs energy-adjusted intake: 3–5 knots at conventional percentiles (3 knots at 10/50/90, or 4 at 5/35/65/95)
notes: One-liner 1559-1560; term 1579-1580; voice.py:1583-1591; WHAT_EXPLORATION_MAY_DECIDE.md:132. The test checks placement against R, not the adequacy of the k rule.

statement: A p for linear trend across quintiles, computed with each quintile's median as a continuous score rather than the quintile number, tests that the outcome rises linearly across quintile medians and is not a test of a dose–response.
decision: the trend test reported beside quintiles
user_sees: A test that the outcome rises linearly across quintile medians; it is not a test of a dose–response.
notes: Drawer 1592-1596; voice.py:1592-1593. test_form_3_5_tests_and_quintiles.py::test_5_the_p_for_linear_trend... checks the arithmetic.

statement: Held-out rows give one honest performance number only if nothing was tuned against them, so they are scored once; a holdout re-drawn after an opening is not an independent test; and the held-out report needs both discrimination (C-statistic with interval) and calibration (intercept, slope, curve, Brier score).
decision: opening the seal and re-sealing
user_sees: Held-out rows give one honest number only if nothing was tuned against them.
notes: voice.py:2225-2227 and 2249-2251. Seal-guard tests (test_wp16_seal_guards.py) test behavior, not the claim.

statement: When a positive outcome is analyzed on the natural-log scale, a coefficient is a difference in mean log and its exponential a ratio of geometric means, and under prediction the exponential of a prediction estimates the geometric mean (the median when the log is normal), not the mean.
regime: positive, skewed outcome on the log scale
decision: the outcome-scale methods sentence
user_sees: a coefficient is a difference in its mean log, and its exponential a ratio of geometric means
notes: For a continuous predictor the exponential is a multiplicative change in the geometric mean per unit. BEATS_PREDICT ruling 2 rejects a log scale for glucose.

statement: Above 10,000 analyzed rows, the substitution band's bootstrap draws about 10,000 rows' worth of whole units per resample and rescales its spread by √(m/n), m and n counted in units, which recovers the full-sample band (an m-out-of-n bootstrap).
decision: the band's resampling
user_sees: drawn as whole units where a unit has several rows, the band's spread rescaled by √(m/n) to the full sample (an m-out-of-n bootstrap)
notes: test_substitution.py::test_a_band_from_fewer_units_than_there_are_is_rescaled_to_all_of_them checks the scale factor only. √(m/n) assumes a √n-rate statistic; for a percentile band the rescaling about the center is an approximation.

statement: Rows that are imputed copies of one record (e.g., NHANES DXA's five imputations) are, under inference, each analyzed as a completed dataset and the estimates pooled by Rubin's rules, which carries the imputation's uncertainty.
regime: inference; rows read as imputed copies
decision: how imputed copies are analyzed
user_sees: each copy is analyzed as a completed dataset with its own outcome and the estimates pooled by Rubin's rules, which carries the imputation's uncertainty (NCHS's combining rules)
notes: Contradicts the teaching option (content.py:541-543: 'under inference kept only as a recorded limitation'). Rubin's rules carry the imputation uncertainty properly only if the provider's imputation was proper and congenial with the analysis.

statement: Under Predict, when the table has a period column, sealing the latest period whole is Recommended (temporal validation; the period is never a predictor for a later moment of use), with development estimated by internal–external cross-validation over the other periods, and a random lockbox only otherwise, justified as protection against the analyst's own choices rather than by Steyerberg 2018.
decision: the seal's Recommended option under Predict
user_sees: The latest survey cycle, whole: 2,270 people (Recommended: "Your model will be used after 2018, and the latest cycle is the nearest thing to that")
claimed_basis: Steyerberg & Harrell 2016; Cawley & Talbot 2010; Gelman & Loken 2013; TRIPOD+AI 12a (§9 rulings 3 and 7)
notes: §9 rulings 3 and 7 (lines 1146-1158, 1182-1183); beat W (lines 348-386). Conflicts with content.py SINGLE_SPLIT ('a single split is the weakest', D-018). The engine cannot draw it yet (C13).

statement: For a model used later than its data, when the latest development period's out-of-period mean error has a 95% interval excluding zero, the final model's intercept is re-estimated in-sample on that period with its coefficients kept (temporal recalibration), because using the out-of-period shift itself as the update would fit to the check.
regime: prediction; later moment of use; data spanning periods
decision: the plan's level rule
user_sees: If the latest development cycle runs above or below its estimates, its level is reset there before the sealed cycle opens.
claimed_basis: Booth et al. 2020; Janssen et al. 2008 (§9 ruling 10, line 1194)
notes: The interval-excludes-zero trigger is a significance gate whose power depends on the period's size.

statement: Values filled before the table was made by an unrecorded method are read as missing and re-imputed in each training fold at the median without indicators, because their missingness belongs to the upstream process, not the person, and does not exist at the moment of use.
regime: prediction; provider-imputed values flagged in the table
decision: First look's filled-values decision
user_sees: "Read them as missing" (Recommended): "Each is filled again in each training fold, from the other people's values and never from glucose."
notes: Beat D (lines 272-346). If the upstream filling depended on the person (e.g., a cuff failing on large arms), the missingness is informative about the person.

statement: For a numeric outcome under Predict every family estimates the conditional mean, so squared error (consistent for the mean) is the one yardstick for comparing, choosing and judging, with verdicts as paired differences in squared miss with intervals, while the mean absolute error (consistent for the median) is description only.
decision: the yardstick for every verdict and choice
user_sees: Judged by its squared miss, said in mg/dL beside a model that estimates everyone at the average: a big miss counts for more than a small one.
notes: §17 ruling 6. Huber regression is on the shelf (beat M3), and it does not estimate the conditional mean under asymmetric errors.

statement: A c statistic of 0.80 or more 'ranks them well', 0.70 to 0.80 'fairly' and below 0.70 'poorly' (Hosmer, Lemeshow & Sturdivant 2013), and a clinical-cut-off range is judged by c and by the share at or above the cut among estimates at or above it, never by a count placed at the cut.
regime: prediction; outcome with a clinical cut-off
decision: verdict words for the diabetic range
user_sees: "It ranks them well (c 0.82), and 4 in 10 of the people it estimates at 126 mg/dL or more are there."
notes: Hosmer–Lemeshow's bands are 0.7–0.8 'acceptable', 0.8–0.9 'excellent', ≥0.9 'outstanding'; the app's words map them differently. 'A count at the cut rewards spread' has no source.

statement: Families whose paired difference in cross-validated MSE from the best lies within 5% of the best family's gain over the no-predictor model are 'equally good', 'not distinguishable' is never read from an interval crossing zero alone, and among them the simplest whose fit raised no concern is the final model (ridge here, because least squares' spline coefficients are poorly determined at scaled condition number 4,229).
decision: the Recommended final model
user_sees: "The three missed alike: on 10 rounds of 5 groups, each differs from the best by less than a twentieth of what the best adds over the average."
claimed_basis: Nadeau & Bengio 2003; TRIPOD+AI 22; Hoerl & Kennard 1970; §17 ruling 6
notes: R4 card (lines 897-905: 'Least squares ... its equation would not hold up'). The 5% margin is a convention; ill-conditioning affects coefficient stability, not predictions within the data's support.

statement: Internal–external cross-validation across survey cycles is summarized by random-effects meta-analysis of the log MSE with a Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman interval and a prediction interval for a new cycle on t(k − 2), because on the identity scale cycles with larger MSE have larger standard errors and so less weight, which is optimistic.
decision: the development estimate across cycles
user_sees: for a new cycle, 24.4 to 42.0 (95% prediction interval)
claimed_basis: Riley et al. 2016; Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009; IntHout et al. 2014; Snell et al. 2018
notes: With k = 8 cycles τ² is imprecise. The engine serves the identity scale today (P27).

statement: Under Predict, each continuous predictor of least squares, ridge and the elastic net enters as a restricted cubic spline (Harrell's knots, placed in each training fold) by default when Riley's sample-size criteria hold for the terms it makes (here 3,916 rows needed for 73 terms at an expected shrinkage of at least 0.9).
decision: the curves default
user_sees: the 73 terms this makes; 3,916 would be enough.
notes: The capture adopted it after a cross-validated benchmark (stated). Riley's criteria count parameters, while ridge and the elastic net change the effective degrees of freedom.

statement: People selected by a high measured outcome sit above the average of people like them, so even a perfectly calibrated model's estimates fall well below their measured values (about 56 mg/dL here); this is regression to the mean, not a bias recalibration would fix, and a clinical range is never judged by the miss among people picked by their measured value.
regime: prediction; outcome with a clinical cut-off
decision: the 'where it misses' verdict rule
user_sees: That is not a bias a recalibration would fix: anyone picked out by a high measurement sits above the average of people like them, so a perfectly calibrated version misses them by 56 too
notes: §6 item 3 (line 1051).

statement: A calibrated model's estimates, being averages for people like each person, spread less than the outcome, with a standard deviation about √R² times the outcome's, and they are said to lie 'in a narrow band' when their SD is under half the outcome's.
decision: the 'how good it is' reading
user_sees: An estimate of the average for people like each person spreads less than the outcome, by about the square root of R² (0.39 × 35 ≈ 14).
notes: §6 item 2 (line 1045). SD(Ŷ) = √R²·SD(Y) holds exactly for in-sample least squares and for E[Y|X] in the population; out of sample, with shrinkage or miscalibration, it is approximate.

statement: Calibration is said 'right on average through the middle' when the calibration slope's interval includes 1, the intercept's includes 0 and E90 is under 5% of the outcome's mean; a slope below 1 means 'its estimates are too spread out' and above 1 'not spread out enough'.
decision: calibration verdict words
notes: The 5%-of-mean E90 threshold is unsourced; an interval including 1 or 0 is an absence-of-evidence reading.

statement: Grouped SHAP values and accumulated local effects describe how a model turns measures into estimates, not what changing a measure would do; within a group of correlated inputs the split of credit is arbitrary, and one input's share is said to be unstable when the reseeds' rank correlation is under 0.7.
decision: the 'what drives it' reading
user_sees: These describe how each model turns measures into estimates, not what changing a measure would do.
claimed_basis: Lundberg & Lee 2017; Apley & Zhu 2020; Molnar et al. 2022
notes: §6 item 6 (line 1067); FOUNDATION §8 floor. The 0.7 threshold is unsourced.

statement: NHANES asks whether someone takes a prescribed medicine only after they were told to take it, so a blank means 'not asked' and is kept as its own level; filling it with the most common answer would mark everyone not asked as taking it, and complete cases would keep only those asked both questions, selected by their diagnoses.
decision: how the medicine answers enter the model
user_sees: Filled with the most common answer, all of them would read as taking it; kept only where both were answered, 2,996 people would remain, chosen by their diagnoses.
claimed_basis: NHANES BPQ questionnaire; Sperrin et al. 2020; Sisk et al. 2023 (§9 ruling 1)
notes: coach.py:316-330 ('This fill gives n not-asked `meds_hbp` blanks `1`'). Under Estimate the same answers 'mark the diagnosis' and are not adjusted for (BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:283).

statement: A prediction model that reads a predictor known only after its intended moment of use looks better in a paper than in use, so only predictors recorded at that moment are read (e.g., no 24-hour recall for a clinic use).
regime: prediction; intended use and moment of use
decision: which columns are predictors
user_sees: A model that reads something known only after its moment looks better in a paper than in use (PROBAST, Wolff et al. 2019, item 2.3).

statement: Under Predict, energy adjustment and substitution are not asked, because the energy model decides what a nutrient's coefficient means (an estimation question) and models that keep total energy predict alike; nutrients enter as recorded beside total calories.
decision: whether the energy question is asked
user_sees: For prediction, models that keep total energy predict alike. (methods/dietary_caveats.py:47-48)
notes: 'Predict alike' holds for linear models with the same column space (standard and linear residual), not for density, log-residual or nonlinear learners.

statement: For a least-squares estimate on an outcome with a clinical cut-off c, writing y = min(y, c) + max(y − c, 0) splits the coefficient exactly into a part from values above the cut and a part from values below, which add to the primary's coefficient, and the estimate is 'mostly the tail' when the part above is more than half and its interval excludes zero.
regime: inference; linear model; outcome with a clinical cut-off
decision: the 'typical person, or the tail?' standing question
user_sees: "The typical person, or the tail?" "Mostly the tail: the diabetic range."
claimed_basis: linearity of least squares in y (no source)
notes: The additivity is exact for OLS. 'From values in the diabetic range' attributes the part to people above the cut, but it is the clipped excess above c among everyone.

statement: The E-value is not reported for a markedly skewed outcome (skew 4.6) because its conversion from a standardized mean difference is meant for a roughly normal outcome; the robustness value (Cinelli & Hazlett) is reported instead, benchmarked only on the adjustment criterion's confounders and never as a pass or fail.
regime: inference; observational design; continuous skewed outcome
decision: the hidden-cause standing question
user_sees: "Could a hidden cause explain it?" "Not ruled out: one tied to both about three times as strongly as survey cycle would erase it."
notes: That the nutrients defining the comparison 'benchmark no hidden cause' is a design choice.

statement: Under Estimate in a same-visit design, answers that NHANES asks only after a diagnosis mark the diagnosis and are not adjusted for as covariates, and reverse causation through a diagnosis (diet changed after it) is a standing question, checked by fitting within those with and without the marker.
regime: inference; exposure and outcome from the same visit; a skip-pattern diagnosis marker
decision: the adjustment set and the reverse-causation check
user_sees: "NHANES asks the medicine questions only of people told they have high blood pressure ... So the answers are not adjusted for: they mark the diagnosis."
notes: Stratifying on a diagnosis marker can itself induce selection bias, since the marker may follow from both diet and the outcome; the doc says 'never proof'.

statement: Results wording starts at the design's floor, an association for an observational design; causal wording is offered only for trials, 'an estimated effect, its assumptions named' only when no standing question points elsewhere and no stated assumption is refuted, and model explanations are never worded as effects.
decision: the drafted wordings and the noticing on stronger user wording
user_sees: "Between groups of people observed as they were: an association, not what would happen if anyone changed their diet."
notes: BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:501, 683; content.py:404-411. It is in tension with the causal lane (DML/TMLE), which offers effect estimates in observational data under declared assumptions.

statement: Showing an eventual outcome's own distribution in Your data before it is named cannot steer a choice toward a result, because a look at one column shows no association and no score.
regime: Your data stage, before the outcome is named
decision: Your data draws every column, the eventual outcome included
user_sees: A look at one column shows no association and no score, so it cannot steer a choice toward a result
notes: WHAT_EXPLORATION_MAY_DECIDE.md's 'Outcome alone' row says a univariate view of Y may not choose the loss, the family or a transform by its shape. Seeing Y's distribution can steer those choices (Gelman & Loken), so the doc's own rule table contradicts 'cannot steer'.

statement: Views that never use the outcome may shape the representation (transforms, knots, filters, imputation rules), and under inference steps learned without the outcome may be fit on the full analysis sample; views that use the outcome may only add candidates to a declared search under prediction (never prune it) and under inference are reported, not acted on, unless a declared selection-aware method carries them.
regime: exploration (First look and Explore) across purposes
decision: what an exploration thread may feed (enforced at registration)
claimed_basis: Harrell RMS 4.7; Baillie 2022; Gelman & Loken 2013; Belloni et al. 2014; Ambroise & McLachlan 2002
notes: UNDERSTANDING_LAYER.md §0 item 5 (enforced when a thread registers). §1 also requires each rule to be declared before the data judge it, rerun in every resample, and its uncertainty carried.

statement: Choosing a robust loss changes the estimand from the mean to the median, and zero inflation cannot be judged from a raw histogram of the outcome, so the outcome's own distribution may not choose the loss or the model family.
decision: what a view of Y alone may decide
notes: §5 item 8. The absolute (L1) loss targets the median, but a Huber loss (the shelf's robust regression, BEATS_PREDICT M3) targets neither mean nor median under asymmetric errors.

statement: Collinearity among predictors is a weak cue for prediction because predictions are unaffected when new data share the collinearity, and under inference exposure–confounder collinearity does not bias a correctly specified model, so it is a causal-diagram question rather than a reason to penalize the exposure.
regime: correlated predictors; cue cards proposing model families
decision: which families the cue cards propose
notes: In tension with content.py:1182-1183 (penalization 'essential when predictors are many or correlated') and the model-family why ('An elastic net ... suits diets where nutrients travel in foods').
